sections.title: Mate
sections.summary: The drink that runs the country

classes.title: What is mate?
classes.summary: A bitter herb, a gourd and a whole lot of history

pages.title: Not a drink. A ritual.
pages.body: **Mate** is hot water poured over **yerba mate**, the dried, ground leaves of a holly tree that grows in the northeast. You sip it through a metal straw from a small cup that's *also* called a **mate**. Then you refill it and pass it to the next person. That's the whole trick, and Argentines do it all day long.
pages.fun_fact: Since 2013, a national law officially names mate Argentina's *infusión nacional*.

pages.statement: In Argentina, the word "mate" can mean both the drink and the cup you drink it from.
pages.explain: Exactly. "Pasame el mate" can mean the cup, the drink, or both. Context does the rest.

pages.title: The Guaraní got there first
pages.body: Long before the Spanish showed up, the **Guaraní** people of what is now Paraguay, northeast Argentina and southern Brazil were drinking the leaf. In Guaraní the plant is **ka'a** and the drink is **ka'ay**, roughly "yerba water". So when you drink mate, you're joining a tradition that is centuries older than Argentina itself.

pages.title: Jesuits, plantations, and a name
pages.body: In the 1600s, **Jesuit** missions in Guaraní lands figured out how to *grow* yerba on plantations instead of harvesting it wild. For a while people even called it "Jesuit tea". The word **mate** itself is usually traced to Quechua **mati**, meaning gourd, the cup that holds it. Today yerba is grown mainly in **Misiones** and **Corrientes**.
pages.fun_fact: November 30 is the Día Nacional del Mate, the birthday of Andrés "Andresito" Guacurarí, a Guaraní leader who governed Misiones.

pages.prompt: Which people first drank yerba mate?
pages.explain: The Guaraní. The Spanish and the Jesuits came later and turned it into a big business.

pages.prompt: Match the word to where it comes from

pages.scenario: You're new in Buenos Aires. A coworker says: "¿Tomás mate?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
options: If you drink mate, and probably offering you one
pages.explain: Mate uses **tomar** (to drink), not *beber*. And the question is usually an invitation. Say **dale** and you're in.

pages.statement: Yerba mate is a kind of green tea from China.
pages.explain: Totally different plant. Yerba mate (*Ilex paraguariensis*) is a South American holly. It does have caffeine, which is why half the country runs on it.

classes.title: The gear
classes.summary: Mate, bombilla, termo, yerba: your starter kit

pages.title: The mate (the cup)
pages.body: The classic one is a dried **calabaza** (gourd). There are also wooden ones, glass, ceramic, steel, and the chunky leather-wrapped **mate camionero**, the "trucker's mate". A new gourd has to be **curado** (cured) first: you fill it with wet yerba and leave it a day or so, so it doesn't taste funky or crack.

pages.title: The bombilla
pages.body: The **bombilla** is a metal straw with a filter at the bottom, so you drink the water and not the leaves. Usually steel or alpaca (a nickel-silver alloy), sometimes fancy silver. It goes in once and stays put. It is not a spoon, and it is definitely not a stirring stick.

pages.statement: If the mate is getting clogged, it's fine to stir the yerba with the bombilla.
pages.explain: Moving the bombilla wrecks the setup and clogs it more. If it's blocked, tell the cebador. It's their mate, their problem.

pages.title: The termo and the yerba
pages.body: The **termo** (thermos) keeps water hot for hours, which is why you see people carrying one under their arm in the park. At home it's the **pava** (kettle). **Yerba** comes in 500 g or 1 kg packs, **con palo** (with stems, milder) or **sin palo** (just leaves, stronger). Everyone swears by their brand, and people can get *very* loyal about it.

pages.prompt: Match the gear to what it does

pages.scenario: At the supermarket you see "yerba con palo" and "yerba sin palo".
pages.prompt: What's the difference?
pages.explain: **Palo** means stick or stem. Stems make it milder and slower to wash out. **Sin palo** hits harder.

pages.prompt: Your friend is about to pour water from the stove. What do you ask for?
pages.text: Pasame la ___, que el agua ya está.
pages.translation: Pass me the kettle, the water's ready.
pages.explain: The **pava** is the kettle. No, you don't use it to drink.

pages.statement: You should wash a brand-new gourd with soap and use it right away.
pages.explain: New gourds get **curados** (cured) with wet yerba first. Soap and gourds don't mix.

classes.title: How to cebar
classes.summary: Making mate, step by step, without embarrassing yourself

pages.title: Cebar: the verb that matters
pages.body: **Cebar** means to prepare and serve mate: pour the water, hand it over, get it back, repeat. The person doing it is the **cebador** (or **cebadora**). It's a small job with big status. A good cebador is appreciated; a bad one hears about it, lovingly, all afternoon.

pages.title: The montañita
pages.body: Fill the mate about ¾ with yerba. Cover the mouth with your hand, flip it, shake, and tilt it so the yerba slides to one side. That slope is the **montañita** (little mountain). You pour into the low side and keep the top dry, so the mate keeps its flavor longer.

pages.prompt: Prepare a mate, step by step
items: Fill the mate about ¾ with yerba
Cover it, flip it, shake it
Tilt it to make the montañita
Wet the low side with a bit of warm water
Put in the bombilla on the wet side
Pour hot water, not boiling, next to the bombilla
pages.explain: The warm water first lets the yerba swell before the hot water hits it. The bombilla goes in once and stays there.

pages.title: Hot, but never boiling
pages.body: The golden rule: the water should be hot, around **70 to 80 °C**, and never boiling. Boiling water **quema la yerba** (burns the yerba) and makes it bitter and harsh. Old-school trick: turn off the pava when it starts to hum, right before the bubbles come.
pages.fun_fact: Many electric kettles in Argentina have a "mate" setting for exactly this.

pages.scenario: The pava is bubbling hard, full boil. Your friend is waiting with the mate ready.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Let it cool down a bit first
pages.explain: Boiling water burns the yerba. You'll hear "¡lo quemaste!" and you'll deserve it.

pages.title: Who drinks the first one?
pages.body: The first mate is often bitter, a bit foamy, and full of dust, so the **cebador** usually drinks it, or spits it out. It's a small sacrifice, not a privilege. After a lot of rounds the flavor fades and the mate is **lavado** (washed out). Then the cebador changes the yerba, or adds a little on the side.

pages.statement: The cebador gives the first mate to the most important guest, as an honor.
pages.explain: Usually the opposite: the first one is the harsh one, so the cebador takes the hit. There is even a saying: **el primero es para el zonzo** (the first one is for the fool).

pages.prompt: The mate has lost all its flavor. What do you say?
pages.translation: Hey, this mate is washed out.
pages.explain: **Lavado** means it's lost its flavor. Time for fresh yerba.

vocabulary.en: the slope of yerba in the mate
to burn the yerba (with boiling water)

classes.title: The rules of the ronda
classes.summary: Mate etiquette, so nobody gives you the look

pages.title: The ronda
pages.body: When people share mate, there's one mate, one bombilla, and one **ronda** (round). The **cebador** fills it and hands it to one person. That person drinks *all* of it until it gurgles, and hands it back to the cebador. Not to their neighbor. Back. Then the cebador fills it for the next one, always in the same order.

pages.scenario: You just finished your mate. The person next to you is looking at it hopefully.
pages.prompt: Who do you give it to?
pages.explain: Always back to the **cebador**. They refill it and pass it on. The mate never skips the cebador.

pages.scenario: Someone hands you a mate and the montañita looks kinda off, the bombilla a bit crooked.
pages.prompt: Should you fix it?
options: No, only the cebador touches it
pages.explain: Hands off. Fixing someone's mate is like rearranging their kitchen while they cook. Just drink it.

pages.title: Gracias means "I'm out"
pages.body: This one catches every foreigner. In a ronda, saying **gracias** when you hand the mate back doesn't mean "thanks", it means "thanks, **I'm done**". Say it after your first mate and you won't get another. Want to keep going? Just hand it back, maybe with a smile or a "¡qué rico!".

pages.statement: If you want more mate, you should say "gracias" every time it's handed to you, to be polite.
pages.explain: Classic trap. **Gracias** = I'm done. Say it only when you want out of the ronda.

pages.title: It's not a microphone
pages.body: Don't hold the mate while you tell a long story. The whole ronda is waiting, and the water is getting cold. Someone will say **"¡No es un micrófono!"** and everyone will laugh at you, kindly. Drink it all, hand it back. And don't complain that it's too hot or too bitter: you're a guest in someone else's mate.

pages.prompt: Your friend is talking and holding the mate forever. What do you say?
pages.translation: Come on, it's not a microphone.
pages.explain: The classic line for someone who hogs the mate.

pages.scenario: You're at a friend's place. You've had four mates and you've had enough.
pages.prompt: What's the smoothest way out?
options: Just stop drinking and hold it
Pass it to the next person
pages.explain: **Gracias** as you hand it back, and the cebador skips you from then on. Easy.

pages.prompt: One turn in the ronda, in order
items: They hand it to you, bombilla facing you
You drink it all, until it gurgles
You hand it back to the cebador
The cebador fills it for the next person

pages.statement: Wiping the bombilla before you drink from it is normal and polite.
pages.explain: Sharing the bombilla is the whole point, and wiping it can come off as a bit of an insult. If you're sick or don't want to share, just say **no, gracias** from the start. That's totally fine.

vocabulary.note: Only say it when you want out.

classes.title: Mate every day
classes.summary: Sweet or bitter, cold or cooked, everywhere you go

pages.title: Amargo or dulce?
pages.body: Most people drink it **amargo** (bitter, no sugar). **Mate dulce** has sugar or sweetener added, more common in some provinces and families. It's a friendly rivalry, not a war. Some purists will tease you, though. People also add **yuyos** (herbs) like peperina or burrito, or a bit of orange peel.

pages.scenario: The cebador asks: "¿Amargo o dulce?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
pages.explain: **Amargo** is no sugar, **dulce** is with sugar. Both answers are OK, but amargo gets you more street cred.

pages.title: Mate cocido
pages.body: **Mate cocido** is the lazy (and cozy) version: yerba in a tea bag, or boiled and strained, served in a regular cup. Often with milk and sugar. It's the drink of school breakfasts, afternoon **merienda**, and cold winter mornings. No bombilla, no ronda, no rules.

pages.title: Tereré: the cold one
pages.body: **Tereré** is mate with cold water or juice, often with ice and herbs. It's huge in **Paraguay**, where UNESCO listed it as cultural heritage in 2020, and in hot provinces like Corrientes, Misiones, Chaco and Formosa. In Buenos Aires you'll see it on summer days, but the hot mate never really takes a vacation.

pages.prompt: Match the drink to what it is
pairs: yerba in a cup, like tea

pages.title: Where? Everywhere.
pages.body: In the office, at university, on a road trip (the co-pilot serves), in the park, at the beach. You'll see people walking with the termo under their arm. **Matear** means to drink mate, and **una matera** is the bag to carry the kit. Uruguayans drink even more per person than Argentines, which they will happily remind you.

pages.statement: Tereré is mostly linked to Paraguay and the hot northeast of Argentina.
pages.explain: Right. In Paraguay it's practically sacred, and in Corrientes or Misiones summer, hot mate can feel like a punishment.

pages.scenario: You're on a road trip. The driver says: "Cebame uno."
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Prepare a mate and hand it to them
pages.explain: The co-pilot is the cebador. Keep them coming, and don't burn the driver.

pages.prompt: Inviting a friend over for mate
pages.translation: Want to come over for mate?
pages.explain: **Matear** = to drink mate, usually together. It's a whole social plan.

vocabulary.en: mate made like tea, in a cup

example.en: Shall we have mate in the park?

vocabulary.en: bag for carrying the mate kit

sections.title: Asado
sections.summary: Fire, meat and a whole Sunday with your people

classes.title: More than a barbecue
classes.summary: Why an asado is a whole afternoon, not a meal

pages.title: It's not just meat
pages.body: An **asado** is grilled meat, sure. But mostly it's an excuse to spend hours together. Sunday lunch with the family, Friday night with friends, a birthday, a work thing — you name it, there's an asado. When someone says **¿hacemos un asado?** (shall we do an asado?), they're really asking: *wanna hang out all day?*
pages.fun_fact: Argentines also say **asado** for a specific cut: the ribs. Context tells you which one.

pages.title: Clear your schedule
pages.body: Nobody does a quick asado. Someone lights the fire late morning, the meat cooks slowly, you eat around two, and then comes the **sobremesa** — sitting at the table long after the food is gone, talking, joking, arguing about football. Getting up at five is totally normal. Leaving right after eating? A bit rude.

pages.statement: At an asado, it's normal to eat and head home half an hour later.
pages.explain: The **sobremesa** is half the point. Leaving right after the food looks like you only came to eat.

pages.title: The asador
pages.body: Every asado has one **asador**: the person in charge of the fire and the meat. Traditionally it's the dad, the uncle, the friend who "knows". It's a role with a lot of pride attached. People hang out next to the grill with a drink to keep the asador company — the grill is where the party starts.

pages.scenario: Everyone's finished eating. The meat was great. Someone at the table raises their glass and shouts something.
pages.prompt: What do they probably shout?
pages.explain: **¡Un aplauso para el asador!** — a round of applause for the grill master. Everyone claps. It's a must, even when the meat was a bit dry.

pages.prompt: Complete the classic toast
pages.translation: A round of applause for the grill master!
pages.explain: Always **asador**. **Mozo** is a waiter, and nobody calls the uncle at the grill a *chef*.

pages.scenario: Your Argentine coworker texts you on Thursday: "¿Hacemos un asado el domingo?"
pages.prompt: What should you plan for?
options: A quick lunch, back home by 2
pages.explain: An invitation to an asado is an invitation to the whole afternoon, at someone's house. Bring good vibes and no plans for later.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning
pairs: chatting at the table after eating

example.en: Shall we do an asado on Sunday?
A round of applause for the grill master!

vocabulary.en: long chat at the table after the meal

example.es: Mañana hacemos un asado en casa.
example.en: Tomorrow we're having an asado at home.

classes.title: Playing with fire
classes.summary: Parrilla, fogón, leña, carbón — and hands off

pages.title: Parrilla or fogón?
pages.body: The **parrilla** is the grill: an iron grate over the embers, often built into the backyard in brick. The **fogón** is an open fire on the ground — think countryside, camping, or a whole lamb on an iron cross leaning over the flames, called **asado a la cruz**. City asados are almost always on a parrilla.
pages.fun_fact: Many Buenos Aires apartments have a small parrilla on the balcony or rooftop. Priorities.

pages.title: Embers, not flames
pages.body: Here's the secret: you don't cook over flames. You cook over **brasas** (embers). The asador burns wood or charcoal on the side, then shovels the glowing embers under the grill, little by little. Slow heat, lots of patience. If you see flames licking the meat, something went wrong.

pages.statement: A good asado is cooked over big, tall flames so it's done fast.
pages.explain: It's cooked slowly over **brasas** (embers). Flames burn the outside and leave the inside raw.

pages.title: Leña vs carbón
pages.body: **Leña** is firewood — hardwoods like quebracho or algarrobo. It takes longer but many swear it gives better flavor. **Carbón** (charcoal) lights faster and is easier, so it's what most people use in the city. Which is better? Ask two Argentines and you'll get three opinions. It's a real, ongoing debate.

pages.prompt: Match the fire words

pages.scenario: You're keeping the asador company. The fire looks a bit weak and there's a pile of wood right next to you.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Throw a couple of logs on to help
Poke the embers around a bit
Nothing — the fire belongs to the asador
pages.explain: Hands off. Only the asador touches the fire and the meat. If you want to help, ask **¿te ayudo en algo?** (can I help with anything?) and do what they say.

pages.prompt: Offer your help the right way
pages.translation: Can I help you with anything?
pages.explain: **¿Te ayudo en algo?** — polite, friendly, and it leaves the asador in charge.

vocabulary.note: Also a restaurant that serves grilled meat.

example.es: Poné más brasas debajo del vacío.
example.en: Put more embers under the flank.

vocabulary.en: whole animal roasted on an iron cross by the fire

classes.title: What comes off the grill, and when
classes.summary: Picada, achuras, then the big cuts

pages.title: First, the picada
pages.body: While the fire does its thing, there's a **picada**: a board with cheese, salami, olives, bread, maybe peanuts. It keeps everyone alive for the first couple of hours. Don't fill up on it, though — you've got a long way to go.

pages.title: Then, the achuras
pages.body: Next come the **achuras** (offal) and sausages: **chorizo** (pork sausage), **morcilla** (blood sausage), **chinchulines** (crispy small intestines), **mollejas** (sweetbreads) and **riñones** (kidneys). They come off in waves, often cut up on a board and passed around. Try the mollejas with lemon. Thank me later.
pages.fun_fact: Technically chorizo and morcilla are sausages, not offal, but at the grill everyone lumps them in with the achuras.

pages.prompt: Match the achura to what it is

pages.title: Finally, the cuts
pages.body: Then the main event, the **cortes** (cuts): **asado de tira** (short ribs cut across the bone), **vacío** (flank), **entraña** (skirt steak, juicy and loved), **matambre** (a thin cut between the skin and the ribs). The asador decides the order. Your job is to eat and say **¡qué rico!** (so good!).

pages.prompt: Put a classic asado in order
items: Picada while the fire gets going
Vacío, entraña and asado de tira
pages.explain: Every family does it a bit differently, but it goes: snacks, sausages and achuras, the big cuts, the applause, and then hours of chatting.

pages.scenario: Someone passes you a board with little golden, crispy spirals. They say: "Probá los chinchulines."
pages.prompt: What are you about to eat?
pages.explain: **Chinchulines** are beef small intestines, grilled until crispy. Sounds scary, tastes amazing. Saying **no, gracias** is fine too.

pages.title: How do you like it?
pages.body: The asador might ask how you want your meat. **Jugoso** means juicy, pink inside. **A punto** is medium. **Cocido** is well done. Most Argentines like it a punto or a bit jugoso. Asking for it very rare? You'll get a raised eyebrow.

pages.prompt: Ask for your meat medium
pages.explain: **A punto** = medium. **Jugoso** if you want it pinker, **cocido** if you want it well done.

pages.statement: Vacío and entraña are types of achuras.
pages.explain: They're **cortes** (cuts of beef). Achuras are the offal: chinchulines, mollejas, riñones… plus the sausages.

example.es: Para mí, a punto, por favor.

classes.title: Choripán, provoleta and the sauces
classes.summary: The sandwich, the grilled cheese and what goes on top

pages.title: The choripán
pages.body: **Choripán** = **chorizo** + **pan** (bread). A grilled sausage, split open in a crusty roll. That's it, and it's perfect. It's the first thing out at many asados, and it's also street food: outside football stadiums, at protests, on the Costanera. Everyone calls it **chori**.

pages.prompt: What's a choripán made of?
pages.text: Un choripán es un chorizo en ___.
pages.translation: A choripán is a chorizo in bread.
pages.explain: **Chori** + **pan**. The name is the recipe.

pages.title: The provoleta
pages.body: **Provoleta** is a thick round of provolone-style cheese grilled until crispy outside and melty inside, with oregano and chili flakes on top. It's usually credited to Natalio Alba, an Italian immigrant, in the mid-20th century. Eat it hot and fast, straight from the little pan.

pages.title: Chimichurri and salsa criolla
pages.body: Two sauces rule. **Chimichurri**: parsley, oregano, garlic, chili flakes, vinegar and oil. **Salsa criolla**: chopped tomato, onion and bell pepper in vinegar and oil. Both go on the choripán and the meat. Where does the name chimichurri come from? Nobody knows for sure — Basque, Italian, even an Irishman called "Jimmy"… all unproven.

pages.prompt: Match the thing to what's in it

pages.statement: Historians agree that chimichurri was named after an Irishman called Jimmy McCurry.
pages.explain: It's one popular story, but it's not proven. Others point to a Basque word or to Italian sauces. The origin is still disputed.

pages.scenario: You're at a football match in Buenos Aires. Outside the stadium, smoke everywhere and people lining up at a street grill.
pages.prompt: What are they most likely selling?
pages.explain: The **chori** is the king of street food at stadiums. Cheap, fast, and you eat it standing up with chimichurri dripping everywhere.

example.en: Shall I make you a chori?

classes.title: You're invited — now what?
classes.summary: What to bring and how not to annoy the asador

pages.title: Never show up empty-handed
pages.body: The host usually buys the meat. You bring something else: **vino** (wine, often a Malbec), **bebida** (drinks: soda, beer, fernet), **postre** (dessert — ice cream is a classic), or **hielo** (ice, and someone always forgets it). Just ask: **¿qué llevo?** (what should I bring?).
pages.fun_fact: With friends, it's common to split the cost of the meat. That's called **hacer una vaquita** — literally "making a little cow".

pages.scenario: Your friend's family invited you to their Sunday asado. You ask what to bring and they say "nada, vení" (nothing, just come).
pages.prompt: What do you actually do?
options: Show up with nothing — they said so
Bring a kilo of steak for yourself
pages.explain: "**Nada, vení**" is being polite. A bottle of wine or some dessert is always welcome. Bringing your own meat can look like you don't trust the host.

pages.prompt: Ask what you should bring
pages.translation: What should I bring to the asado?
pages.explain: **¿Qué llevo?** — the classic question. Argentines use **llevar** (take) from the guest's point of view.

pages.title: The golden rule
pages.body: Don't tell the asador how to cook. Not "it needs more heat", not "I'd flip that now", not "in my country we…". The grill is their territory. Keep them company, bring them a glass of wine, laugh at their jokes. Criticizing the asado is almost a personal insult.

pages.scenario: You think the vacío has been on too long. The asador turns and asks: "¿Todo bien?"
pages.prompt: Best answer?
options: "I think it's burning, you should take it off"
Grab the tongs and take it off yourself
pages.explain: **Huele bárbaro** = it smells amazing. Trust the asador — and never grab the tongs. The meat and the fire are theirs.

pages.statement: Offering to help clear the table or wash up after the asado is a nice gesture.
pages.explain: The asador cooked, so others often clean up. Offering to help with the dishes always earns points.

pages.prompt: A perfect guest's afternoon
items: Keep the asador company at the grill
pages.explain: Nail these and you'll be invited back next Sunday.

pages.prompt: Match what you bring

sections.title: Fútbol
sections.summary: Not a sport here. A religion with a fixture list.

classes.title: ¿De qué cuadro sos?
classes.summary: The five big clubs, the Superclásico and the question you can't dodge

pages.title: The question
pages.body: Meet someone new in Buenos Aires and within ten minutes you'll hear: **¿De qué cuadro sos?** — *Which team are you?* A **cuadro** is a club. It's not small talk: your club is inherited from your dad, your grandpa, your barrio. People change jobs, partners, even countries. Changing clubs? Never. **Cambiar de cuadro** is basically treason.
pages.fun_fact: Plenty of babies are signed up as club members (**socios**) days after being born.

pages.title: Los cinco grandes
pages.body: Five clubs are called **los cinco grandes** — *the big five*: **Boca Juniors**, **River Plate**, **Independiente**, **Racing Club** and **San Lorenzo**. They have the most fans and, historically, the most titles. Everyone else is a *chico* (small club) — though say that to a fan of Vélez or Estudiantes and you'll get a long lecture.

pages.prompt: Match the club to its nickname
pages.explain: **Xeneize** means *Genoese*: Boca was founded in 1905 by Italian immigrants' kids in La Boca. River got **Millonario** for spending big on players in the 1930s.

pages.title: El Superclásico
pages.body: **Boca vs River** is the **Superclásico** — the biggest rivalry in the country. A **clásico** is any derby; this one gets the *super*. Boca plays at **La Bombonera** (*the chocolate box*) in La Boca. River plays at **El Monumental** in Núñez. Funny detail: River was also born in La Boca, in 1901, and moved north later. Neighbors first, enemies forever.
pages.fun_fact: In 2018 they met in the Copa Libertadores final, and the second leg ended up being played in Madrid. River won.

pages.title: Insults with pride
pages.body: Rivals give each other nasty nicknames, and fans end up wearing them proudly. River fans call Boca fans **bosteros** (from **bosta**, *manure* — the story goes it was a dig at the smell by the Riachuelo). Boca fans call River fans **gallinas** (*chickens*, as in cowards), a name that stuck after River blew the 1966 Libertadores final against Peñarol. San Lorenzo fans are **cuervos** (*crows*), after the priest who founded the club.

pages.statement: If a River fan calls you a "bostero", they think you support Boca.
pages.explain: Exactly. And if you *do* support Boca, the correct reply is a proud smile. Being **bostero** is a badge of honor for them.

pages.title: Avellaneda: two stadiums, one block
pages.body: Just south of the city, in **Avellaneda**, live **Racing** (light blue and white) and **Independiente** (red). Their stadiums are only a few hundred meters apart — you can see one from the other. That's the **clásico de Avellaneda**. Independiente fans are the **Diablos Rojos**, *Red Devils*. Imagine sharing a street with the one team you hate most.

pages.scenario: You're staying in La Boca and a friend lends you a red-and-white River shirt because it's cold. You're about to walk to the kiosk next to the Bombonera on match day.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Wear it, it's just a shirt
Wear it, but say you're a tourist
pages.explain: Never wear the rival's colors in the wrong barrio, especially on match day. Best case: jokes and dirty looks. Worst case: you really don't want to find out.

pages.scenario: A taxi driver asks: "¿De qué cuadro sos?" You don't follow football at all.
pages.prompt: What's the smoothest answer?
options: Pick the rival of whatever sticker is on his dashboard
pages.explain: Turning the question back is gold: he'll happily talk for the whole ride. Saying football is boring is legal, but it's a conversation killer.

pages.prompt: Ask your new friend which team they support
pages.translation: Which team are you (a fan of)?
pages.explain: **Cuadro** is the everyday word for club. **Cuadra** is a city block — useful, but not here.

vocabulary.note: Boca, River, Independiente, Racing, San Lorenzo.

vocabulary.en: Boca fan (rivals' insult, worn with pride)

vocabulary.note: Don't say it to a River fan unless you're friends.

example.en: Shall we go to the match on Sunday?

classes.title: La hinchada
classes.summary: Chants, drums and the mysterious thing called aguante

pages.title: Hincha, not fan
pages.body: A fan is a **hincha**, and all the fans together are **la hinchada**. The story goes that the word comes from a man in Montevideo who inflated (**hinchar**) the balls and shouted so hard he became famous. Whatever the origin: a hincha doesn't *watch* a match. A hincha *plays* it from the stands.
pages.fun_fact: **Hinchar** also means to annoy. "No me hinchés" = "Stop bugging me."

pages.title: Cantitos and the bombo
pages.body: The stands never go quiet. The hinchada sings **cantitos** (*chants*) for ninety minutes, often to the tune of old rock or cumbia songs, with lyrics that mix love for the club and creative insults for the rival. Keeping the beat is the **bombo**, a big bass drum. Add **trapos** (*banners*) and paper rain, and you've got the show.

pages.statement: In an Argentine stadium, fans sit quietly and clap after good plays.
pages.explain: Sitting? Quietly? In the **popular** (standing terraces) people jump, sing and push for the whole match. Clapping politely is for tennis.

pages.title: El aguante
pages.body: **Aguante** comes from **aguantar**, *to endure*. For a hincha it means loyalty that survives everything: rain, losses, even relegation. "**¡Aguante Racing!**" = *Long live Racing!* You also hear it outside football: "**¡Aguante el asado!**" The team can be losing 3–0 and the hinchada still sings — that's aguante.

pages.prompt: Cheer for your team, rioplatense style
pages.translation: Long live Boca! / Come on Boca!
pages.explain: **¡Aguante…!** + anything you love. It works for clubs, bands and even foods.

pages.title: The dark side: barras bravas
pages.body: Every big club has a **barra brava** (or just **la barra**): the organized hardcore group that leads the chants and carries the drums. Many are also tangled up in violence and shady business — resale, parking, politics. After years of deaths, visiting fans were banned from most matches in 2013. Pilot tests to bring them back only began in 2025.

pages.scenario: At the stadium, a guy from the barra walks past and tells your section to stand up and sing.
pages.prompt: What's the smart move?
options: Explain that you paid for your seat
Stand up and at least pretend to sing
pages.explain: You're a guest in their church. Stand, clap, hum along. Arguing with the barra is never a good plan.

pages.prompt: Match the word to the thing
pages.explain: **Trapo** literally means *rag*. For the barras, losing your trapo to a rival is the ultimate humiliation.

pages.statement: If your team gets relegated, a real hincha with aguante stops going to the stadium.
pages.explain: The opposite! When River went down in 2011, its fans filled stadiums in the second division. Aguante is exactly for the bad times.

classes.title: 1978, 1986 and the Diez
classes.summary: The first two World Cups and a guy called Diego

pages.title: La Selección
pages.body: When Argentina plays, the whole country stops. The national team is **la Selección**, or **la Albiceleste** (*the white and sky-blue*). Club rivalries freeze for ninety minutes — a bostero and a gallina hug when Argentina scores. The team has won three World Cups: **1978**, **1986** and **2022**.

pages.title: 1978: a cup with a shadow
pages.body: Argentina hosted and won in **1978**, beating the Netherlands 3–1 after extra time at El Monumental, with two goals from **Mario Kempes**. But the country was under a military dictatorship that used the cup as propaganda while people were disappearing. Many Argentines still feel torn about it. Some results, like the 6–0 over Peru, remain the subject of suspicion that was never proven.

pages.statement: Everyone in Argentina celebrates the 1978 World Cup without mixed feelings.
pages.explain: The players are respected, but the dictatorship context makes 1978 a sore, debated topic. Tread gently.

pages.title: Diego
pages.body: **Diego Armando Maradona** grew up poor in Villa Fiorito and became the greatest idol the country has ever had. He wore the **10**, so he's **el Diez** — or simply **el Diego**. He captained Argentina to the **1986** title in Mexico. Some people even joke about the *Iglesia Maradoniana*, a fan "church" with its own Christmas on his birthday, October 30.

pages.title: Mexico 1986 vs England
pages.body: Quarter-final, June 22, 1986, four years after the Falklands/**Malvinas** war. Minute 51: Diego punches the ball into the net and the referee allows it. He later called it **la Mano de Dios** — *the Hand of God*. Four minutes later he dribbles past half the English team from his own half and scores **el Gol del Siglo**, *the Goal of the Century*. Argentina won 2–1.
pages.fun_fact: Radio commentator Víctor Hugo Morales screamed "¡Barrilete cósmico!" — *cosmic kite* — and it became legend.

pages.prompt: Put Argentina vs England, 1986, in order
items: Maradona dribbles past five players and the keeper
pages.explain: The Hand of God and the Goal of the Century were only four minutes apart. Gary Lineker scored England's goal near the end.

pages.scenario: An English friend at an asado says: "Maradona cheated, that's it." Everyone goes quiet.
pages.prompt: How do most Argentines see the Mano de Dios?
options: A shameful moment they'd rather forget
A cheeky bit of viveza, with a lot of history behind it
pages.explain: For many it's **viveza criolla** (street-smart cunning) and a symbolic revenge after Malvinas. Plenty of people also admit it was a handball. Expect a passionate debate, not agreement.

pages.prompt: What's the famous handball called?
pages.explain: **Mano** is feminine even though it ends in -o: *la mano*.

pages.statement: Argentina won the 1986 final against West Germany.
pages.explain: 3–2 in the Azteca stadium. Jorge Burruchaga scored the winner after a pass from — who else — Diego.

vocabulary.en: the Hand of God (1986 handball goal)

vocabulary.note: Admired and criticized in equal measure.

classes.title: Messi and Qatar
classes.summary: Heartbreak in Brazil, glory in Qatar

pages.title: The quiet kid from Rosario
pages.body: **Lionel Messi** was born in **Rosario** in 1987 and left for Barcelona at 13. For years some Argentines grumbled that he didn't sing the anthem and only shone in Spain. He's a **Newell's** fan, by the way, and nicknamed **la Pulga** (*the flea*) for being small. That grumbling is now very, very dead.

pages.title: 2014: so close
pages.body: The **2014** final in Rio's Maracanã: Argentina vs Germany, 0–0 into extra time. In minute 113, **Mario Götze** scored. Germany 1–0. Messi was named best player of the tournament and looked at the trophy he couldn't touch. Then came two lost Copa América finals, in 2015 and 2016. After 2016, Messi briefly retired from the Selección.

pages.statement: Argentina lost the 2014 World Cup final to Brazil.
pages.explain: It was **Germany**, 1–0, played in Brazil. Losing in Brazil's own stadium, to anyone, stung extra.

pages.title: Qatar 2022
pages.body: December 18, 2022. The final against France was madness: Argentina 2–0, then Mbappé scores twice in two minutes, Messi makes it 3–2 in extra time, Mbappé again: 3–3. Penalties. **Dibu Martínez**, the **arquero** (*goalkeeper*), saves one, and **Gonzalo Montiel** scores the last. Messi finally lifts the cup. Argentina's third star.
pages.fun_fact: The celebration in Buenos Aires drew millions of people — the Obelisco disappeared under a sea of shirts.

pages.prompt: Put the Qatar 2022 final in order
pages.explain: 4–2 on penalties. Many Argentines say they didn't breathe for about three hours.

pages.title: Muchachos
pages.body: The soundtrack of Qatar was a cantito: **"Muchachos, ahora nos volvimos a ilusionar"** — *Guys, now we've got our hopes up again*. Fans wrote it to the tune of a song by the band La Mosca. It name-checks Malvinas, Diego and Leo. Sing it at any party and the whole room joins in.

pages.scenario: It's a Selección match day and your Argentine friend has worn the same unwashed socks for every game since the tournament started.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: It's a cábala — a lucky ritual
pages.explain: A **cábala** is a superstitious ritual. Same seat, same socks, same mate. If the team wins, you do NOT change anything.

pages.prompt: Match the hero to the moment
pages.explain: Four finals, four names every Argentine knows — including the German one, sadly.

pages.prompt: Your friend is scared to change his lucky socks. He says:
pages.translation: I'm not washing them, it's a lucky ritual.
pages.explain: **Mufa** is bad luck (or the person who brings it) — the exact opposite.

example.es: El Dibu es el mejor arquero.

vocabulary.note: Plural: penales. "Ir a penales" = go to a shootout.
La final = the final match. El final = the ending.

classes.title: Talk like a hincha
classes.summary: Golazos, gambetas, caños and the Sunday picado

pages.title: Potrero and picado
pages.body: Argentines say their football was born in the **potrero** — a dirt lot where kids play with a ball, a couple of stones as goalposts and zero rules. A casual game with friends is a **picado**. "¿Armamos un picado?" = *Shall we get a game together?* Today it's usually **fútbol 5** on synthetic grass, then beers.
pages.fun_fact: Calling a player "**de potrero**" is a big compliment: street-smart, creative, fearless.

pages.title: Gambeta and caño
pages.body: A **gambeta** is a dribble, the twisty, dancing kind Maradona and Messi made famous. A **caño** is a nutmeg: the ball between the defender's legs. Getting a caño in a picado means your friends will remind you for weeks. And a **golazo** is a stunning goal. The **-azo** ending makes anything bigger: **golazo**, **partidazo**.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning

pages.scenario: In a picado, you slip the ball between the legs of your friend Nacho and run past him. Everyone screams.
pages.prompt: What did you just do?
pages.explain: **¡Caño!** Nacho will now be teased until the next picado. Maybe longer.

pages.title: El DT and the arquero
pages.body: The coach is **el DT** (*de-té*), short for **director técnico**. Every Argentine is secretly a DT: they all know who should play. The goalkeeper is **el arquero** (from **arco**, *goal*). And the defender who kicks everything out? A **hachero** — an *axe man*.

pages.statement: In Argentina, "el DT" is the team's doctor.
pages.explain: **DT** = **director técnico**, the coach. Lionel Scaloni, the DT who won Qatar, gave his name to the team's nickname: **la Scaloneta**.

pages.title: Hacer la previa
pages.body: Before any big match you **hacer la previa**: meet up earlier to eat, drink, sing and get in the mood. The previa can last longer than the match itself. After the game, win or lose, there's analysis at the bar until late. Watching football alone? Suspicious behavior.

pages.prompt: Invite your friends to meet up before the Superclásico
pages.translation: Shall we do the pre-match hangout at my place?
pages.explain: Careful: a **picada** is a snack board of cheese and salami — very welcome at the previa, but not the same word.

pages.prompt: A perfect Superclásico Sunday, in order
items: Analyze every play at the bar

pages.scenario: Your team lost 4–0. Your Argentine friend's phone keeps buzzing with memes from rival fans.
pages.prompt: What's the local tradition here?
options: Mute everyone and disappear until Monday
Take the gastada, then return it when your team wins
pages.explain: A **gastada** is the teasing after a loss. You take it, you keep a list, and you pay it back with interest.

example.en: Shall we get a game together?

vocabulary.en: dirt lot where kids play football
to hang out before an event

example.es: Hacemos la previa en lo de Juan.
example.en: We're meeting at Juan's place first.

sections.title: Alfajores y dulces
sections.summary: Dulce de leche, kioscos and the snack that runs on sugar

classes.title: What is an alfajor?
classes.summary: Two cookies, dulce de leche in the middle, and a thousand years of history

pages.title: The national snack
pages.body: An **alfajor** is two soft cookies (**tapas**, literally 'lids') glued together with **dulce de leche**, usually dipped in chocolate. That's it. That's the whole religion. We eat them at the office, on the bus, after football, at 2am. If an Argentine offers you half their alfajor, that's basically friendship.
pages.fun_fact: Industry estimates say Argentines eat around six million alfajores a day. Nobody has counted properly — we were busy eating.

pages.title: Not born here, though
pages.body: Plot twist: the alfajor isn't Argentine by birth. The word comes from Andalusian Arabic — most sources trace it to **al-hasú**, 'the filling'. In Muslim Spain (al-Ándalus) it was a honey, almond and spice sweet. It's still made in Andalucía today. The Spanish brought the name to the Americas, and here it turned into cookies plus dulce de leche.
pages.fun_fact: The exact Arabic root is debated — some say al-fasur, some al-hasú. Everyone agrees it's Arabic.

pages.statement: The alfajor was invented in Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: The name and the idea come from al-Ándalus, Muslim Spain. Argentina just made it its own — and, humbly, perfected it.

pages.title: The family tree
pages.body: Each region has its own. **Alfajor de maicena**: crumbly cornstarch cookies, dulce de leche, edges rolled in **coco rallado** (grated coconut) — the homemade one your abuela makes. **Marplatense**: chocolate-coated, from Mar del Plata, the classic kiosco one. **Santafesino**: crunchy layers with a white sugar glaze. **Cordobés**: soft, glazed, often filled with fruit jam.

pages.prompt: Match the alfajor to what makes it special
pairs: soft and filled with fruit jam
dipped in chocolate, the kiosco classic

pages.title: More is more
pages.body: Then there's the **triple**: three tapas, two layers of dulce de leche. More alfajor per alfajor. And the **alfajor de fruta**, filled with **membrillo** (quince paste) or other jams instead of dulce de leche — the cordobés tradition. The **simple** is the regular two-tapa one. When you ask for one at a kiosco, you'll hear: '¿Simple o triple?'

pages.scenario: You had a long day, skipped lunch, and you're at a kiosco with exactly enough coins for one alfajor.
pages.prompt: What do you ask for?
pages.explain: Triple. Three tapas, double dulce de leche. It's lunch now. Nobody will judge you.

pages.prompt: Your abuela's homemade alfajores have coconut on the sides. What are they?
pages.explain: **Maicena** is cornstarch. The cookies crumble in your hand and the coconut ends up everywhere. Worth it.

pages.prompt: Build an alfajor de maicena
items: Spread dulce de leche on one
Put the other tapa on top
Roll the edges in grated coconut
pages.explain: Four steps. Abuela does it in two seconds and without a recipe.

example.es: Mi abuela hace alfajores de maicena.

classes.title: Brands, kioscos and the eternal debate
classes.summary: Havanna or Jorgito? Pick a side at the kiosco on the corner

pages.title: The kiosco
pages.body: Every block has one. A **kiosco** is a tiny shop — sometimes just a window — selling candy, drinks, cigarettes, phone credit and, above all, alfajores. Many stay open late; some never close (look for the **24 hs** sign). The bigger ones are **maxikioscos**. The person behind the counter is the **kiosquero**, and they know your order.
pages.fun_fact: The **ventanita** kiosco is literally a window in someone's house. Knock, ask, pay, done.

pages.scenario: It's 1am, you're walking home from a party and you desperately want something sweet.
pages.prompt: Where do you go?
pages.explain: The kiosco. Late hours are its whole personality. Look for the light on and the '24 hs' sign.

pages.title: The heavyweights
pages.body: **Havanna**: born in Mar del Plata in 1947, the fancy one you bring as a gift. **Jorgito** (1960): the working-class hero. **Guaymallén** (1945): cheap, humble, legendary — 'el alfajor de la familia'. **Fantoche**: famous for its triple. Then there's **Capitán del Espacio**, a cult classic; **Cachafaz**, premium and named after a tango dancer; and the big-company ones, **Terrabusi** and **Milka**.

pages.statement: Havanna is from Mar del Plata, the beach city.
pages.explain: Founded in 1947 in Mar del Plata. Coming back from the coast without a box of Havanna is borderline illegal.

pages.scenario: You're visiting your Argentine partner's family for the first time and you pass through Mar del Plata on the way.
pages.prompt: What do you bring?
pages.explain: A box of Havanna is the classic regalo. Guaymallén is beloved, but it's a coins-in-your-pocket snack, not a meet-the-parents gift.

pages.title: The debate that never ends
pages.body: Ask a table of Argentines 'which is the best alfajor?' and clear your afternoon. Some swear by Havanna. Others say Havanna is overpriced and the real deal is a Jorgito or a **Guaymallén blanco** (the white sugar-glazed one). There is no right answer. Well — there is, it's yours, and everyone else is wrong.
pages.fun_fact: For about two decades, Jorgito and Fantoche kept an unwritten pact: Jorgito ruled Buenos Aires, Fantoche the rest of the country. So the story goes, at least.

pages.prompt: Match the brand to its reputation
pairs: the fancy gift from Mar del Plata
premium, named after a tango dancer

pages.title: The World Cup of alfajores
pages.body: Yes, it exists. The **Campeonato Mundial del Alfajor** started in Buenos Aires in 2022. Hundreds of alfajores, a blind tasting, a serious jury of pastry chefs. Most winners are small artisan makers, not the big brands. In 2026 the top prize went to El Rodeo, from Catamarca: fig filling, walnuts and a glaze with coconut.
pages.fun_fact: Argentina hosting a 'world' championship for its own snack and winning it every year is peak Argentina.

pages.prompt: At the kiosco, you want two alfajores. Ask for them.
pages.translation: Can you give me two alfajores?
pages.explain: **¿Me das…?** with **vos** is the natural, friendly way. 'Dais' is from Spain — not here, ever.

vocabulary.en: corner shop for candy, drinks and snacks

example.en: I'm going to the kiosco, want anything?

vocabulary.en: alfajor with a white sugar glaze

example.en: I brought you Havanna as a gift.

vocabulary.en: Can I have…? / Can you give me…?

classes.title: Dulce de leche and friends
classes.summary: The spread on everything, and the sweets it hangs out with

pages.title: The brown gold
pages.body: **Dulce de leche** is milk and sugar cooked slowly for hours until it turns thick, brown and caramel-y. We put it on toast, in cakes, in alfajores, on a spoon straight from the jar at midnight. It's not 'caramel'. Don't call it caramel. An Argentine will correct you, gently, for twenty minutes.

pages.title: The legend
pages.body: The story goes like this: 1829, the ranch La Caledonia in Cañuelas. Rosas and his enemy Lavalle meet to sign a truce. A maid is heating milk with sugar for Rosas's mate, gets distracted by the drama, forgets the pot — and finds it turned into dulce de leche. Cute story. Almost certainly a legend: Uruguay, Chile, France and others claim it too.

pages.statement: Historians agree dulce de leche was invented in Argentina in 1829.
pages.explain: The Cañuelas story is a legend. Similar milk sweets existed elsewhere, and Uruguay in particular will fight you on this. Just enjoy it.

pages.title: Clásico vs repostero
pages.body: At the supermarket you'll see two kinds. **Clásico** (or **familiar**) is soft and spreadable — for toast and the spoon. **Repostero** is thicker and firmer, made for baking: it holds its shape inside alfajores and cakes without dripping everywhere. **Repostería** means pastry-making, hence the name.

pages.scenario: You're making alfajores and the filling keeps oozing out the sides.
pages.prompt: What did you buy wrong?
options: You used clásico — you needed repostero
You used repostero — you needed clásico
pages.explain: Repostero is firmer and stays put. Clásico is for the tostada and the spoon.

pages.title: The supporting cast
pages.body: **Chocotorta**: Chocolinas cookies dipped in milk, layered with dulce de leche mixed with cream cheese. No oven, every birthday. **Pastafrola**: a tart with a lattice top, filled with membrillo or **batata** (sweet potato) jam. **Mantecol**: a peanut nougat bar people get weirdly emotional about. **Bon o Bon**: a little chocolate bonbon with peanut cream, a kiosco staple.

pages.prompt: Match the sweet to what it is
pairs: lattice tart with quince or sweet potato jam

pages.prompt: Make a chocotorta
items: Mix dulce de leche with cream cheese
Layer cookies and cream, again and again
Put it in the fridge for a few hours
pages.explain: No oven needed. That's why every Argentine kid's birthday has one.

pages.prompt: Your friend asks what you want on your toast.
pages.explain: **Obvio** is how we say 'obviously' — and for the toast, it's obvio.

example.es: Le pongo dulce de leche a todo.
example.en: I put dulce de leche on everything.

vocabulary.en: no-bake chocolate cookie and dulce de leche cake

classes.title: Facturas: anarchy at the bakery
classes.summary: Medialunas, bolas de fraile and the rebel bakers who named them

pages.title: What are facturas?
pages.body: **Facturas** are the pastries you buy at the **panadería** (bakery), usually by the **docena** (dozen) in a paper bag. They're the official partner of mate. Afternoon at a friend's place? Someone shows up with a dozen facturas. It's the law. (Yes, 'factura' also means invoice. Context helps.)

pages.scenario: Your friend texts: 'Venite a tomar mate a las 5.'
pages.prompt: What do you bring?
pages.explain: Facturas. Mate at 5pm plus a dozen facturas is the most Argentine afternoon there is. Wine is for the asado.

pages.title: Manteca or grasa?
pages.body: The queen is the **medialuna** ('half-moon', a small croissant). Two kinds: **de manteca** (butter) — sweeter, glazed, curved; and **de grasa** (beef fat) — drier, a little salty, usually straight. You order them by name: 'media docena de manteca'. Debating which is better is another national sport.

pages.statement: A medialuna de grasa is the sweet, glazed one made with butter.
pages.explain: That's the **de manteca**. **Grasa** means fat — beef fat — and those are saltier and less sweet.

pages.title: Rebel bakers
pages.body: In 1887 Buenos Aires bakers, many of them Italian and Spanish anarchists, founded their first union. The story goes that they named pastries to mock the powers of the day: the **vigilante** (police) is long like a cop's baton; **bolas de fraile** ('friar's balls') and **suspiros de monja** ('nun's sighs') poke the Church; **cañoncitos** ('little cannons') and **bombas** the army.
pages.fun_fact: Historians debate how much of this is documented, but it's the story every baker will tell you.

pages.prompt: Match the factura to who it teases

pages.title: Order like a local
pages.body: At the panadería you ask for a mix: 'Una docena surtida' — a dozen assorted. Or you pick: 'Seis medialunas y seis facturas'. **Bolas de fraile** are fried dough balls filled with dulce de leche or pastry cream. **Cañoncitos** are puff pastry tubes filled with dulce de leche. Fight for the last one.

pages.prompt: You want twelve mixed facturas. Ask the baker.
pages.explain: **Surtida** = assorted. The baker picks a bit of everything, and you look like you've lived here for years.

pages.prompt: The perfect afternoon, in order
items: Everyone fights over the last cañoncito

pages.scenario: At the table, only one factura is left. Your friend says 'dale, comela vos'.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: They're offering you the last one
pages.explain: **Dale, comela vos** = 'Go on, you eat it.' The last factura is a sacred and delicate thing. Accept gracefully.

example.en: I'll bring pastries for the mate.

sections.title: Puteadas
sections.summary: Argentine swearing: what it means, and when to keep your mouth shut

classes.title: Boludo, the word that does everything
classes.summary: Greeting, insult, punctuation: one word, many jobs

pages.title: Welcome to the puteadas
pages.body: Grab a mate. In Argentina a **puteada** is a swear or an insult, and **putear** is to swear at someone (or at the universe). Argentines swear a lot, and often with love. This section teaches you to *understand* them, and, more importantly, when *not* to use them.
pages.fun_fact: You'll hear more swearing in a Buenos Aires café than in most bars back home.

pages.title: Boludo
pages.body: **Boludo** (**boluda** for a woman) literally means 'big-balled', i.e. an idiot. But between friends it softened into 'dude' or 'mate'. **¿Qué hacés, boludo?** is just 'What's up, man?'. Same word, said slowly with a stare, is still an insult: 'you idiot'. Tone and relationship decide everything.
pages.fun_fact: Some porteños use it so often it's basically a comma: 'Fui al súper, boludo, y no había nada, boludo.'

pages.scenario: Your friend Nico sees you at the bar, grins and shouts: '¡Boludo! ¿Qué hacés acá?'
pages.prompt: Is Nico insulting you?
options: No, he's happy to see you
pages.explain: Warm tone plus a friend = **boludo** means 'dude'. He's just surprised to see you there.

pages.scenario: Your brand-new boss, on your first day, says: 'Che, boludo, pasame eso.'
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: He's being overly casual: odd, but probably not an insult
It's the formal way to talk at work
pages.explain: Probably not an insult: some people use **boludo** with anyone. But it's very casual for a boss, and it's never the 'formal' option. Don't say it back until you know him well.

pages.title: Pelotudo: the upgrade
pages.body: **Pelotudo** comes from **pelotas** (balls, again) and means 'idiot' too, but stronger. It's rarely affectionate. **¡Qué pelotudo!** = 'What an idiot!'. A silly or trivial thing is a **boludez** or **pelotudez**: 'Es una boludez' = 'It's nothing / it's a dumb little thing'.

pages.statement: Pelotudo is the friendly, softer version of boludo.
pages.explain: It's the other way around. **Boludo** can be friendly; **pelotudo** almost always stings.

pages.prompt: Your friend apologizes for spilling a bit of mate. How do you say 'Don't worry, it's nothing'?
pages.explain: **Boludez** = a trivial thing. Friendly and harmless.

pages.scenario: A stranger bumps into you on the subte and you say '¡Boludo!' with a frown.
pages.prompt: How will he hear it?
pages.explain: No friendship, angry tone: it's an insult. The word didn't change; the context did.

example.en: Girl, you won't believe what happened!
He swore at me in the street.

classes.title: Gil, forro, chanta: the cast of characters
classes.summary: The people Argentines love to complain about

pages.title: The gil
pages.body: A **gil** is a sucker: naive, easy to fool. It's an old lunfardo word from tango days, when the **gil** was the one who got scammed and the **vivo** was the sharp guy. **No seas gil** = 'Don't be a sucker'. Rude, but mild.
pages.fun_fact: Tango lyrics are full of giles who got their heart broken.

pages.title: The chanta
pages.body: A **chanta** is a bullshitter: someone who brags, promises and never delivers. The plumber who says 'mañana vengo' for three weeks? **Chanta**. The guy who claims he played in the Primera? **Chanta**. It comes from **chantapufi**, an Italian-dialect word for someone who doesn't pay his debts.

pages.title: The forro
pages.body: **Forro** literally means 'lining' and is also slang for condom. Called at a person, it means a jerk: someone mean, disloyal or selfish. **Sos un forro** = 'You're such a jerk'. It hurts more than **boludo** because it's about character, not brains.

pages.prompt: Match the character to who they are

pages.scenario: A taxi driver charges you triple because you're a tourist, and you paid.
pages.prompt: What would your Argentine friend call you, lovingly?
pages.explain: You got fooled, so you're the **gil**. The taxi driver is the **chanta** (or the **forro**).

pages.title: The pests
pages.body: Someone who won't stop bugging you is a **hinchapelotas** or **rompebolas**: literally 'ball-swelling' and 'ball-breaking'. Pain in the neck. **Pajero** literally means 'wanker'; among friends it often means lazy or spaced out: **No seas pajero, ayudame** = 'Don't be lazy, help me'. Crude, so keep it among friends.

pages.statement: Calling your friend a 'hinchapelotas' because he texts you 40 times a day is a fair use of the word.
pages.explain: Exactly the right use. Between friends it's a jokey complaint, not a war.

pages.prompt: Your roommate is on the couch while you carry all the groceries.
pages.explain: **Pajero** here = lazy. A **chanta** lies, a **gil** gets fooled.

pages.scenario: Your friend promised to help you move, didn't show up, and posted beach pics that same day.
pages.prompt: Which word fits him best?
pages.explain: Disloyal and selfish: that's a **forro**. A **boludez** is a trivial thing, not a person.

vocabulary.en: wanker; among friends, lazy or spaced out
sharp, street-smart (the opposite of a gil)

classes.title: La puta madre: pure frustration
classes.summary: The exclamations for when everything goes wrong

pages.title: Swearing at the universe
pages.body: Stub your toe, miss the bus, see the inflation numbers: **¡La puta madre!** Nobody's mother is involved; it's just 'Damn it!'. It goes up in levels: **la puta que lo parió** ('the whore who gave birth to it') and the maximum, **la re puta que lo parió**. The **re** means 'really, super'.
pages.fun_fact: People shorten it to just 'La puta…' with a long, tired sigh.

pages.title: The heavy one
pages.body: **¡La concha de tu madre!** is very vulgar (**concha** is vulgar slang for female genitals). Shouted at nobody, after dropping your phone in the toilet, it's frustration. Aimed at a person, it's a serious insult. Fun variant: **la concha de la lora** ('the parrot's...'), pure frustration, no target.

pages.prompt: Order these from mildest to strongest
pages.explain: The euphemism is softest, and aiming a vulgar phrase *at a person* is the strongest of all.

pages.title: Dismissals
pages.body: **¡Andá a cagar!** literally 'go take a shit', means 'get lost'. But between friends it's often disbelief: 'No way!' or 'Shut up!'. And **me chupa un huevo** ('it sucks me an egg', with egg = testicle) means 'I don't give a damn'. The deluxe version: **me chupa un huevo y la mitad del otro**.

pages.scenario: You tell your friend you met Messi at the airport. She laughs and says: '¡Andá a cagar!'
pages.prompt: What does she mean?
pages.explain: Laughing + amazing news = disbelief. Same words, said cold, would mean 'get lost'.

pages.prompt: Your coworker asks if you care who wins the reality show. You really don't.
pages.explain: **Me chupa un huevo** = I couldn't care less. Crude, so coworkers only if you're close.

pages.title: The family-friendly versions
pages.body: Around kids or grandparents? Swap in a euphemism. **¡Miércoles!** ('Wednesday!') stands in for **mierda** (shit). **¡Pucha!** or **¡La pucha!** replaces **la puta**. **Me importa un comino** ('I don't care a cumin seed') replaces the egg one. Same frustration, no scandal.

pages.prompt: Match the polite version to the one it's hiding
pages.explain: Euphemisms sound like the real thing, so everyone knows what you meant, but nobody's offended.

pages.statement: When someone shouts '¡La puta madre!' after missing the bus, they're insulting someone's mother.
pages.explain: It's an exclamation, like 'Damn it!'. No mothers were harmed.

example.en: Damn it, I missed the bus!

vocabulary.es: la re puta que lo parió

vocabulary.en: very vulgar: frustration, or a serious insult at someone
vocabulary.note: Never aim it at a person unless you want a fight.

classes.title: Reading the room
classes.summary: The stadium, the traffic, and your girlfriend's grandma

pages.title: At the cancha
pages.body: The football stadium (**la cancha**) is where swearing becomes a sport. The referee (**el referí**) gets **¡Cobrá, la concha de tu madre!** ('Make the call!'), and a slow striker hears **¡Dale, pelotudo!**. Warning: many stadium chants include slurs about gays, other nationalities and so on. We skip those, and so should you.
pages.fun_fact: The ref is insulted so often that some fans say it's part of the ticket price.

pages.statement: Singing along to every stadium chant is fine, since everyone else is doing it.
pages.explain: Lots of chants are homophobic or racist, and there's growing pushback against them. Cheer, swear at the ref, but skip the slurs.

pages.title: Behind the wheel
pages.body: Buenos Aires traffic turns saints into sailors. The light turns green and someone honks: **¡Dale, boludo!** ('Come on, idiot!'). Somebody cuts you off: **¡Aprendé a manejar!** ('Learn to drive!') or **¿Quién te dio el registro?** ('Who gave you a license?'). Usually it's just venting. Hand gestures can escalate things, so keep yours on the wheel.

pages.prompt: The light turned green five seconds ago and the car in front hasn't moved.
pages.explain: Classic traffic venting. Said to a stranger in a car, **boludo** is an insult, but a very routine one.

pages.title: The abuela test
pages.body: Before you swear, ask: would I say this in front of my girlfriend's grandma? With close friends, **boludo**, **la puta madre** and **andá a cagar** are totally normal. With your boss, your in-laws, a cop or a stranger? Go polite: **¡pucha!**, **¡miércoles!** Swearing badly makes you sound rude; swearing well makes you sound local.

pages.scenario: Sunday lunch with your girlfriend's family. You burn your tongue on the ravioles.
pages.prompt: What do you say?
pages.explain: **La pucha** says 'ouch, darn' without making the abuela drop her fork.

pages.scenario: You're watching the match at a bar with your friends and your team misses a penalty.
pages.prompt: Which reaction fits in?
pages.explain: At a bar with friends during football, full swearing is expected. 'Oh dear' would get you strange looks.

pages.prompt: Order from 'swear freely' to 'keep it clean'
items: Your best friends at the cancha
pages.explain: The closer and more relaxed the relationship, the more puteadas are allowed.

pages.prompt: Match the place to the classic puteada

example.es: Vamos a la cancha el domingo.
example.en: We're going to the game on Sunday.

sections.title: Historia: el nacimiento de un país
sections.summary: From the first peoples to the tango: how Argentina came to be, up to 1930

classes.title: Before Buenos Aires
classes.summary: The first peoples, and a city that had to be founded twice

pages.title: They were here first
pages.body: Long before any Spaniard showed up, this land was full of peoples: the **guaraníes** in the humid northeast, the **diaguitas** farming the valleys of the northwest, the **mapuches** in the south by the Andes, the **tehuelches** across Patagonia, and the **querandíes**, hunters of the pampa right where Buenos Aires stands today. Argentines call them **pueblos originarios** (original peoples).
pages.fun_fact: Iguazú comes from Guaraní and means roughly 'big water'. Fair enough.

pages.prompt: Match each people to where they lived
pages.explain: And the mapuches lived on both sides of the Andes, in the south. The map was never empty.

pages.title: Words that stayed
pages.body: You speak native languages every day here without noticing. From **quechua** (the Andean language of the Inca world): **cancha** (field, court), **choclo** (corn on the cob), **palta** (avocado) and even **mate** — the word first meant the gourd. From **guaraní**: **ñandú** (the local ostrich-like bird) and **yaguareté** (jaguar). So when you ask for a **tostado con palta**, say thanks to the Andes.

pages.scenario: At a parrilla, your friend asks if you want a **choclo** on the grill.
pages.prompt: What are they offering you?
pages.explain: **Choclo** is corn on the cob, a word from quechua. The avocado is **palta** — also quechua, and never 'aguacate' here.

pages.title: Buenos Aires, take one
pages.body: In **1536** the Spaniard **Pedro de Mendoza** founded a settlement on the Río de la Plata and named it after the Virgin of the good winds: **Santa María del Buen Ayre**. It went badly. Hunger, disease and fights with the **querandíes** crushed it, and by **1541** the survivors had abandoned it. Many sailed up the river to Asunción, in today's Paraguay.

pages.title: Take two
pages.body: In **1580**, **Juan de Garay** came down from Asunción and founded the city again — this time for good. That's why porteños talk about **la primera fundación** and **la segunda fundación**. For two centuries it stayed a small, muddy port, more famous for smuggling than for anything else. The real money was in the silver mines of **Potosí**, far up in today's Bolivia.
pages.fun_fact: **Porteño** literally means 'from the port' — that's what people from Buenos Aires are called.

pages.prompt: Put these in order
items: Pueblos originarios live across the land for thousands of years
Pedro de Mendoza founds Buenos Aires (1536)
The first Buenos Aires is abandoned (1541)
Juan de Garay founds it again (1580)

pages.statement: Buenos Aires has survived without interruption since its very first founding.
pages.explain: The first one (1536) was abandoned in 1541. The city that lasted is Garay's, from 1580.

pages.prompt: Your friend is from Buenos Aires. How do they describe themselves?
pages.explain: **Porteño** — from the port. You'll hear it a hundred times a day.

example.es: Los pueblos originarios vivían acá mucho antes.
example.en: Indigenous peoples lived here long before.

example.es: Un tostado con palta, por favor.
example.en: A toasted sandwich with avocado, please.

classes.title: A viceroyalty and two British invasions
classes.summary: How a sleepy port became a capital, and threw out the British twice

pages.title: The Virreinato
pages.body: In **1776** the Spanish crown created the **Virreinato del Río de la Plata** (Viceroyalty of the River Plate), with Buenos Aires as its capital. It covered today's Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia. Overnight the smuggling port became the boss, run by a **virrey** (viceroy) who answered to the king in Spain.

pages.prompt: Which of these countries was NOT part of the Virreinato del Río de la Plata?
pages.explain: Chile was a separate Spanish territory. The Virreinato covered Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia.

pages.title: The Cabildo
pages.body: Every Spanish colonial city had a **cabildo**: the town council, and the building where it met. The one in Buenos Aires is still standing on **Plaza de Mayo**, white, with arches and a little tower. You can visit it — it's a museum now. Look closely: it's shorter than it used to be.
pages.fun_fact: It lost three arches in 1889 to open Avenida de Mayo, and three more in 1931. From eleven arches to five.

pages.title: The British are coming
pages.body: In **1806** a British force under **William Beresford** took Buenos Aires. The viceroy ran away to Córdoba — not his finest hour. Locals organized under **Santiago de Liniers** and kicked the British out that August: the **Reconquista**. In **1807** the British came back, bigger, with **John Whitelocke**. Porteños fought street by street, and won again: the **Defensa**.

pages.title: Hot water from the rooftops
pages.body: The story every Argentine kid learns: during the Defensa, neighbors threw boiling water and oil from the flat rooftops onto the British soldiers. Some of it is legend polished over time, but the street fighting was very real. And the lesson stuck: porteños had beaten an empire without Spain's help. Why keep obeying a viceroy?

pages.statement: When the British took Buenos Aires in 1806, the viceroy led the defense of the city.
pages.explain: Viceroy Sobremonte fled to Córdoba with the treasury. The locals, led by Liniers, did the fighting.

pages.scenario: Walking downtown, you pass a street called **Reconquista**. Later, in San Telmo, you walk down **Defensa**.
pages.prompt: What do those street names remember?
options: The victories against the British invasions
pages.explain: **Reconquista** (1806) and **Defensa** (1807): the two times porteños beat the British. Buenos Aires names its streets after its history.

pages.prompt: Put these in order
items: Juan de Garay founds Buenos Aires
Spain creates the Virreinato del Río de la Plata
The British take Buenos Aires and are expelled (Reconquista)
The British return and lose again (Defensa)

classes.title: May and July: the big dates
classes.summary: The Revolución de Mayo in 1810 and independence in 1816

pages.title: Spain in trouble
pages.body: In 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain and locked up its king. In **May 1810**, news arrived in Buenos Aires that Spain had almost completely fallen. Big question: if there's no king, who's in charge here? On **22 May** the city held a **cabildo abierto** — an open town meeting of leading neighbors — and voted to remove the viceroy.

pages.title: 25 de mayo de 1810
pages.body: On **25 May 1810** a new local government took over: the **Primera Junta** (First Board), led by **Cornelio Saavedra**. It still ruled in the name of the Spanish king, at least on paper, so it wasn't independence yet. But it was the first government chosen here, by people from here. This is the **Revolución de Mayo**, and it's why the main square is called **Plaza de Mayo**.
pages.fun_fact: The classic school drawing shows the crowd with umbrellas. Historians say umbrellas were rare back then — it's probably a myth.

pages.scenario: It's the 25th of May and your friend offers you **locro** (a thick corn-and-meat stew) and **pastelitos** (fried pastries with quince).
pages.prompt: What are you celebrating?
options: The end of the British invasions
pages.explain: The 25th of May is the Revolución de Mayo. Locro and pastelitos are the patriotic menu — you'll see them again on the 9th of July.

pages.title: 9 de julio de 1816
pages.body: Six years of war later, delegates from the provinces met in a house in **San Miguel de Tucumán**, in the northwest. On **9 July 1816** the **Congreso de Tucumán** declared independence from Spain and from any foreign power. The country called itself the **Provincias Unidas en Sud América**. The house is now the **Casa Histórica**, a museum.

pages.statement: Argentina declared its independence in Buenos Aires, on the 25th of May.
pages.explain: Independence was declared in Tucumán, on 9 July 1816. The 25th of May (1810) is the revolution that started the process.

pages.prompt: Match the date to what happened
pairs: Cabildo abierto votes out the viceroy

pages.title: Walk the calendar
pages.body: Buenos Aires is a history book you can walk. **Avenida de Mayo** runs from the Casa Rosada to the Congress. **Avenida 9 de Julio**, the huge one with the Obelisco, is named after independence day. Both dates are **feriados** (public holidays), and almost every town in the country has a street called 25 de Mayo and another called 9 de Julio.

pages.prompt: You're in a taxi and want the widest avenue in town. You say:
pages.text: Vamos a la avenida ___ de Julio, por favor.
pages.translation: Let's go to 9 de Julio Avenue, please.
pages.explain: **9 de Julio**: independence day, and the avenue with the Obelisco.

items: The Congreso de Tucumán declares independence

example.en: Independence is celebrated on the 9th of July.

classes.title: San Martín, Belgrano and the flag
classes.summary: The general who crossed the Andes and the man who made the flag

pages.title: Belgrano's flag
pages.body: **Manuel Belgrano** was a lawyer and economist who ended up a general in the independence wars. On **27 February 1812**, by the Paraná river in **Rosario**, he raised a light blue and white flag for the first time. Buenos Aires wasn't thrilled — it was a bit too independent for 1812. Today Rosario has a giant **Monumento a la Bandera**.

pages.title: Why light blue and white?
pages.body: Kids learn the colors come from the sky and its clouds. Some historians argue they come from the colors of the Spanish royal house of Borbón instead. Nobody can prove either one. Before the flag came the **escarapela**, a light blue and white rosette people pin on their chest on patriotic days. The **sol de mayo** (May sun) in the middle came later.
pages.fun_fact: The 18th of May is Día de la Escarapela. Watch for the rosettes on kids' school uniforms.

pages.statement: Belgrano died a rich and famous man, and that's why his day is a holiday.
pages.explain: He died poor, in Buenos Aires, on 20 June 1820. That date is now Día de la Bandera (Flag Day), a holiday.

pages.title: San Martín crosses the Andes
pages.body: **José de San Martín**, born in **Yapeyú** (Corrientes) and trained as a soldier in Spain, had a bold plan: beat Spain in Peru by going through Chile. From **Mendoza** he built the **Ejército de los Andes** and in **1817** crossed the mountains — thousands of men, mules and horses over passes more than 4,000 meters high. He won at **Chacabuco** and helped free Chile, then Peru.

pages.scenario: You're in the Catedral Metropolitana, next to Plaza de Mayo, and see soldiers in old blue uniforms guarding a tomb.
pages.prompt: Whose tomb is it?
pages.explain: San Martín's mausoleum, guarded by the **Granaderos**, the cavalry regiment he founded. He died in France in 1850; his remains came home in 1880.

pages.prompt: Match the hero to the fact
pairs: raised the first flag in Rosario
crossed the Andes with an army
led the fight against the British in 1806

pages.prompt: Argentines call San Martín the father of the nation:
pages.translation: He's the Father of the Homeland.
pages.explain: **Padre de la Patria**. His day is 17 August, the anniversary of his death — another feriado.

example.en: The 20th of June is Flag Day.
